abstract: Repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) depends on large-scale changes in nuclear shape and genome organization. How damage signaling coordinates such remodeling remains unclear. We find that the human DNA damage response (DDR) couples interdependent, temporally ordered tubulin modifications to nuclear membrane and lipid regulation, driving nuclear reshaping (nucleomorphosis) through DSB-capturing nuclear envelope tubules (dsbNETs). Tubulin detyrosination by vasohibins 1/2 (VASH1/2) and acetylation by -tubulin acetyltransferase 1 (ATAT1) promote dsbNET formation and support both homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining. Microtubule-dependent processes also promote the phosphorylation-dependent inactivation of the membrane stress-sensing lipid regulator CTP cytidylyltransferase- (CCT), which typically restrains baseline nuclear lipid droplets (nLDs) and dsbNETs while supporting ATR signaling. Damage-induced nLD formation requires diacylglycerol acyltransferases 1/2 (DGAT1/2) and supports dsbNETs. Our findings reveal a distributed architectural code spanning interconnected cytoskeletal, membrane, and lipid regulators. This code governs nucleomorphosis and its role in DNA repair and genome stability.
